{{Short description|Special group in linear algebra}}
In algebra, an '''Iwahori subgroup''' is a subgroup of a [[reductive algebraic group]] over a nonarchimedean [[local field]] that is analogous to  a [[Borel subgroup]] of an algebraic group. A '''parahoric subgroup''' is a [[Proper subset | proper]] subgroup that is a finite union of double cosets of an Iwahori subgroup, so is analogous to a [[Borel subgroup|parabolic subgroup]] of an algebraic group. Iwahori subgroups are named after [[Nagayoshi Iwahori]], and "parahoric" is a [[portmanteau]] of "parabolic" and "Iwahori". {{harvtxt|Iwahori|Matsumoto|1965}} studied Iwahori subgroups for Chevalley groups over ''p''-adic fields, and {{harvtxt|Bruhat|Tits|1972}} extended their work to more general groups. 

Roughly speaking, an Iwahori subgroup of an algebraic group ''G''(''K''), for a local field ''K'' with integers ''O'' and residue field ''k'', is the inverse image in ''G''(''O'') of a Borel subgroup of ''G''(''k'').

A reductive group over a local field has a [[Tits system]] (''B'',''N''), where ''B'' is a parahoric group, and the Weyl group of the Tits system is an [[affine Coxeter group]].

==Definition==
More precisely, Iwahori and parahoric subgroups can be described using the theory of affine [[Building (mathematics) | Tits buildings]]. The (reduced) building ''B''(''G'') of ''G'' admits a decomposition into '''facets'''. When ''G'' is [[Quasisimple group | quasisimple]] the facets are [[Simplex | simplices]] and the facet decomposition gives ''B''(''G'') the structure of a [[simplicial complex]]; in general, the facets are polysimplices, that is, products of simplices. The facets of maximal dimension are called the '''alcoves''' of the building.

When ''G'' is [[Reductive group#Definitions | semisimple]] and [[Reductive group#Classification of split reductive groups | simply connected]], the parahoric subgroups are by definition the [[Stabilizer subgroup | stabilizers]] in ''G'' of a facet, and the Iwahori subgroups are by definition the stabilizers of an alcove. If ''G'' does not satisfy these hypotheses then similar definitions can be made, but with technical complications.

When ''G'' is semisimple but not necessarily simply connected, the stabilizer of a facet is  too large and one defines a parahoric as a certain finite index subgroup of the stabilizer. The stabilizer can be endowed with a canonical structure of an ''O''-group, and the finite index subgroup, that is, the parahoric, is by definition the ''O''-points of the [[Glossary of algebraic geometry | algebraic connected component]] of this ''O''-group. It is important here to work with the algebraic connected component instead of the [[Connected component (topology) | topological connected component]] because a nonarchimedean local field is [[totally disconnected]].

When ''G'' is an arbitrary reductive group, one uses the previous construction but instead takes the stabilizer in the subgroup of ''G'' consisting of elements whose image under any [[multiplicative character | character]] of ''G'' is integral.

==Examples==
*The maximal parahoric subgroups of GL<sub>''n''</sub>(''K'') are the stabilizers of O-[[Lattice (module) |lattices]] in ''K''<sup>''n''</sup>. In particular, GL<sub>''n''</sub>(''O'') is a maximal parahoric. Every maximal parahoric of GL<sub>''n''</sub>(''K'') is conjugate to GL<sub>''n''</sub>(''O''). The Iwahori subgroups are conjugated to the subgroup ''I'' of matrices in GL<sub>''n''</sub>(''O'') which reduce to an upper triangular matrix in GL<sub>''n''</sub>(''k'') where ''k'' is the residue field of ''O''; parahoric subgroups are all groups between ''I'' and GL<sub>''n''</sub>(''O''), which map one-to-one to parabolic subgroups of GL<sub>''n''</sub>(''k'') containing the upper triangular matrices. 
*Similarly, the maximal parahoric subgroups of SL<sub>''n''</sub>(''K'') are the stabilizers of O-lattices in ''K''<sup>''n''</sup>, and SL<sub>''n''</sub>(''O'') is a maximal parahoric. Unlike for GL<sub>''n''</sub>(''K''), however, SL<sub>''n''</sub>(''K'') has {{nowrap|''n''}} conjugacy classes of maximal parahorics.
*When ''G'' is [[Algebraic torus | commutative]], it has a unique maximal compact subgroup and a unique Iwahori subgroup, which is contained in the former. These groups do not always agree. For example, let ''L'' be a [[Finite extensions of local fields | finite separable extension]] of ''K'' of ramification degree ''e''. The torus ''L<sup>×</sup>/K<sup>×</sup>'' is compact. However, its Iwahori subgroup is ''O<sub>L</sub><sup>×</sup>/O<sub>K</sub><sup>×</sup>'', a subgroup of index ''e'' whose cokernel is generated by a uniformizer of ''L''.
